items.title: The 7 Factions of the AI Safety Political Universe - Politico
items.summary: When people talk about “AI safety,” this is what they really mean. Brendan Bordelon is POLITICO’s AI and tech influence reporter. In the battle over AI regulation — from Washington, D.C. to Silicon Valley — one term has become unexpectedly controversial: “AI safety.” After all, who doesn’t believe in making these tools safe? “AI safety” is now something of a Rorschach test for how tech founders, politicians and everyone in between thinks about AI development. The technology is still so young that political opinions surrounding AI have yet to be firmly locked in, and it’s possible to find skeptics and boosters on both the left and right. So, we decided to ask 20 of the smartest, most consequential people working in and around the industry the same question: When you hear the phrase “AI safety,” what’s your first reaction and what does it mean to you?

items.title: Did OpenAI's models just breach its own risk 'red line'? Outside safety experts think so - Fortune
items.summary: AI safety experts say the OpenAI models that carried out the autonomous hack of another company earlier this month may have crossed into a risk category so dangerous that OpenAI’s own internal risk control policies were supposed to require the company to temporarily pause development of those models. Several AI safety experts told *Fortune* the recent hack appears to show OpenAI’s models have crossed into a level of risk that OpenAI’s own published safety policies define as “critical,” the highest level of danger. The “critical” threshold is defined in a risk policy document known as OpenAI’s “Preparedness Framework.” According to the policy, the “critical” danger level designation is supposed to apply to a model that can independently find and build working exploits for previously unknown security flaws across many well-defended, real-world systems—or one that can design and carry out an entirely new attack strategy against a well-defended target after being given only a general goal, with no human guidance along the way.

items.title: Stronger AI Safety Requires Peeking Inside the 'Black Box' - Dark Reading
items.summary: Adding security to AI often treats the large language model (LLM) or AI system as a black box, focusing on analyzing the tokenized inputs and outputs but not what goes on inside the model. A group of offensive-security researchers hopes to change that, presenting at the Black Hat USA 2026 in August a model-agnostic approach to activation analysis with standardized rules for processing activation events. The goal is to create an open system of identified cognitive elements and rules that detect specific types of safety events, similar to Snort or YARA rulesets, says Yisroel Mirsky, an assistant professor and head of the Offensive AI Research Lab at Ben-Gurion University of The Negev. Analyzing the tokenized input to or output of a model is similar to antivirus scanning and heuristics — it's fast and catches a wide variety of attacks, raising the bar for attackers, but defense in depth needs more layers, says Mirsky.

items.title: AI Reads Even the 'Context' of Risk… Sage Unveils Next-Generation Industrial Safety Solution - 벤처스퀘어
items.summary: Sage, an industrial AX company, is unveiling an AI safety monitoring solution that understands on-site situations and contexts by applying a Vision Language Model (VLM) specialized for industrial safety. The company is targeting the industrial safety market by highlighting its ability to go beyond simple detection to reduce unnecessary false positives and enable flexible operations tailored to individual company safety standards. SAIGE will participate in the '2026 International Safety and Health Exhibition (KISS 2026),' held at KINTEX in Goyang, Gyeonggi Province from July 6 to 9, and showcase its AI-based safety monitoring solution, 'SAIGE SAFETY.' This year's KISS is the largest industrial safety exhibition in Korea, introducing various AI safety technologies applied to industrial sites under the theme of the 'AI Safety and Health Expo.'. It re-evaluates results initially detected by AI by taking into account the situation and context of the site, focusing on reducing typical false positives in existing AI video analysis, such as misidentifying welding sparks as a fire or mistaking a worker's posture for an accident.

items.title: Weak AI Regulation Is Worse Than No Regulation, Researchers Claim - Gizmodo
items.summary: Game theory says the best AI safety regulation is strict and targets everyone in the supply chain, according to the paper. Weak AI safety regulations may “backfire,” creating a product that is potentially more dangerous than AI products created under no regulation, according to a new study published on Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Using theoretical economics and game theory principles, a group of researchers from Cornell and Carnegie Mellon University created a theoretical model that aims to show how AI regulation can be most effective at ensuring safety. They found that for true safety, regulation needs to be strict while targeting the companies that develop AI models (such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic), rather than solely focusing on the downstream companies that apply the technology in real-life settings, like companies that provide AI medical diagnostic systems or e-commerce customer service chatbots.

items.summary:
Since quantum computers are fundamentally analog machines that are sensitive to drift, maintaining reliable operation requires perpetually recalibrating their control parameters, i.e., the frequencies, amplitudes, and phases of the analog signals choreographing the qubits. Today, this requires fully terminating the entire quantum computation. This complete decoupling of computation and calibration represents a fundamental bottleneck for the future, as useful quantum algorithms must run [...] RL_for _QEC-1

Quantum computation is physically realized via analog control signals. The quantum error detection events are used by the decoder to infer logical corrections. items.title: An ordinary laptop solved a problem thought to require a quantum computer
items.summary:
The challenge involved modeling hundreds of interacting 'qubits,' the quantum counterparts of the bits used by traditional computers. The qubits were arranged in square, cubic, or diamond shaped lattices.

A conventional bit stores either a 0 or a 1. A qubit, however, can exist in a superposition of multiple states. This feature gives quantum systems their unusual capabilities, but it also makes their behavior extremely difficult to reproduce on a classical computer. [...] Summary:
:   A quantum problem once described as impossible for classical computers has now been solved using relatively modest hardware. Researchers used tensor networks to compress the overwhelming wave function created by hundreds of entangled qubits, allowing some calculations to run on a laptop. Their results matched both theoretical predictions and simulations performed with a quantum computer. The method could open new paths for exploring quantum dynamics and materials. [...] By extracting more computing power from conventional hardware, the approach could expand the range of quantum dynamics problems scientists can study. It may also offer a useful strategy for optimization problems in which researchers must identify the best answer among many possible solutions.

The findings were published in the journal Science.
